unesco.title: Al-Razfa, a traditional performing art
unesco.description: Al-Razfa is a traditional performing art practised throughout the United Arab Emirates and the Sultanate of Oman. It is performed by men of all ages and classes during social occasions, such as weddings and national festivals. Male performers form two facing lines with dancers filling the space between. Led by the main singer, the two rows create a dual chorus, singing chants in an antiphonal manner to the accompaniment of drums and other instruments. Many chants are verses of traditional Nabati poetry, carefully selected to match the occasion. The dancers perform choreographed movements to the music while holding wooden replica rifles in their hands and in some cases, young girls swing their hair in time to the music. Originally performed as a communal celebration of victory, Al-Razfa is now widely popular as a form of entertainment. Practitioners have adapted musical instruments and composed melodies to interest younger audiences while maintaining the older expressions and oral traditions of the art. Performers may include heads of State and elders or very young children. Today, Al-Razfa is transmitted directly within the family through participation and observation at social occasions. The roles of individual performers are learnt by practice, while girls receive instruction from their mothers and older sisters.

profile.name: Al-Razfa
profile.tagline: Antiphonal chants and choreographed rifle movements of the UAE and Oman
profile.insight: Once a communal celebration of battle victory, Al-Razfa pairs two facing rows of men chanting Nabati poetry with dancers wielding wooden replica rifles.
profile.profile: Al-Razfa is a traditional performing art practiced across the United Arab Emirates and the Sultanate of Oman. Performed by men of all ages and social classes during weddings and national festivals, the art features two facing lines of performers creating a dual chorus led by a main singer. Dancers move in the space between the rows, executing choreographed movements while holding wooden replica rifles, while young girls sometimes swing their hair to the music. profile.profile_long:
Al-Razfa is a traditional performing art practiced throughout the United Arab Emirates and the Sultanate of Oman. Originally performed as a communal celebration of victory, the dance has evolved into a popular form of social entertainment performed at social occasions such as weddings and national festivals.

The structural formation of Al-Razfa consists of male performers forming two facing lines, with dancers filling the central space between them. Led by a main singer, the two rows establish a dual chorus that sings chants in an antiphonal, call-and-response manner. Many of these chants consist of verses from traditional Nabati poetry, carefully selected to fit the specific occasion.

During the performance, dancers execute choreographed movements while holding wooden replica rifles in their hands. In some instances, young girls participate by swinging their long hair in time to the music. Musicians accompany the singers and dancers using drums and other instruments, with modern practitioners adapting musical instruments and composing new melodies to appeal to younger audiences.

Al-Razfa is inclusive of all ages and social classes, with performers ranging from heads of State and elders to young children. Knowledge and skills are transmitted directly within the family through observation and active participation during social gatherings, where individual roles are learned through practice.

sections.origins_and_history: Al-Razfa originally developed as a communal celebration of victory. Over time, it transitioned from a post-battle ritual into a popular form of social entertainment across the United Arab Emirates and Oman. Modern practitioners have continued to adapt instruments and compose melodies to engage younger audiences while preserving its traditional oral heritage.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Performers arrange themselves into two facing lines, while dancers fill the space in between. Guided by a main singer, the two facing rows sing antiphonal chants to one another. Dancers carry wooden replica rifles and execute choreographed movements to the rhythm, and young girls occasionally swing their hair in time with the music.
sections.music_and_instruments: The musical component relies on a dual chorus singing chants set to traditional Nabati poetry. The vocal performance is accompanied by drums and other instruments, with contemporary artists incorporating updated melodies and musical arrangements.
sections.costume_and_setting: The dance is staged during social occasions, such as weddings and national festivals. Dancers carry wooden replica rifles during the performance, and participating girls swing their long hair to the rhythm.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: While historically performed to mark a victory, Al-Razfa is now performed as social entertainment during national festivals and weddings. It acts as a shared tradition that brings together elders, heads of State, and young children.
sections.notable_figures: Individual roles within the dance are learned through practical experience at social events, with girls receiving instruction directly from their mothers and older sisters.
sections.regional_variants: Al-Razfa is practiced throughout both the United Arab Emirates and the Sultanate of Oman, shared across both nations as part of their intangible cultural heritage.
sections.lineage: Transmission occurs directly within families. Younger generations learn their specific roles through active participation and observation during social gatherings.
